Below are three minimal‑size implementations of an **LRU (Least‑Recently‑Used) cache** – one each for **TypeScript**, **Python**, and **Go**.  
Each version uses only the language’s standard library so they compile/run out‑of‑the‑box.

---

## 1️⃣ TypeScript  

```ts
// Simple LRU Cache implementation (≈30 LOC)

type LRUCache<K, V> = {
  /** capacity of the cache */
  capacity: number;

  /** retrieve a value and mark it as recently used */
  get(key: K): V | undefined;

  /** insert or update a key‑value pair; evict least‑recently used if needed */
  set(key: K, value: V): void;
};

/**
 * Implementation using Map + Doubly‑Linked List.
 *
 * - `map` gives O(1) lookup/insert/delete.
 * - `dll` keeps the order of usage (most recent at head).
 */
class LRUCacheImpl<K, V> implements LRUCache<K, V> {
  private capacity: number;
  private map = new Map<K, { value: V; prev?: Node<K,V>; next?: Node<K,V>}>();
  // dummy nodes for head/tail of the doubly‑linked list
  private head!: Node<K,V>;
  private tail!: Node<K,V>;

  constructor(capacity: number) {
    this.capacity = capacity;
    this.head = { value: undefined, prev: null, next: null };
    this.tail = { value: undefined, prev: null, next: null };
    this.head.next = this.tail;
    this.tail.prev = this.head;
  }

  /** Move a node to the head (most‑recent) */
  private moveToHead(node: Node<K,V>) {
    // detach
    if (node.prev) node.prev.next = node.next;
    if (node.next) node.next.prev = node.prev;

    // attach at head
    node.prev = this.head;
    node.next = this.head.next;
    this.head.next!.prev = node;
    this.head.next = node;
  }

  /** Evict the tail (least‑recently used) */
  private evict() {
    if (!this.tail.prev || !this.head.next) return; // empty or already evicted
    const victim = this.tail.prev!;
    this.remove(victim);
    delete this.map[victim.key];
  }

  /** Remove a node from the doubly‑linked list */
  private remove(node: Node<K,V>) {
    if (node.prev) node.prev.next = node.next;
    if (node.next) node.next.prev = node.prev;
    // head/tail never removed
  }

  get(key: K): V | undefined {
    const entry = this.map.get(key);
    if (!entry) return undefined;

    // promote to most‑recent
    this.moveToHead(entry);

    return entry.value!;
  }

  set(key: K, value: V): void {
    let node = this.map.get(key);
    if (node) {
      // update value & move to head
      node.value = value;
      this.moveToHead(node);
      return;
    }

    // new key – create a fresh node and add it right after head
    const newNode: Node<K,V> = { key, value };
    this.map.set(key, newNode);

    if (this.map.size > this.capacity) {
      // capacity exceeded → evict LRU from tail
      this.evict();
    }

    // insert at head
    node.prev = this.head;
    node.next = this.head.next!;
    this.head.next!.prev = node;
    this.head.next = node;
  }
}

// ----------------------------------------------------
// Example usage

const cache = new LRUCacheImpl<string, number>(3);
cache.set('one',   1);
cache.set('two',   2);
cache.set('three', 3);

console.log(cache.get('one')); // → 1
cache.set('four', 4);          // evicts 'two'
console.log(cache.get('two')); // → undefined

// ----------------------------------------------------
```

**Key points**

* `Map<K, Node>` stores the key‑value pairs plus pointers to a doubly‑linked list node (`Node`).
* `head`/`tail` sentinel nodes simplify insertions/removals.
* `moveToHead()` and `evict()` keep O(1) operations.

## 2️⃣ Python  

```python
from collections import OrderedDict

class LRUCache:
    """
    Simple LRU cache implementation (≈30 LOC).

    - capacity: maximum number of items.
    - get(key): returns value or None if missing.
    - set(key, value): inserts/updates; evicts least‑recently used on overflow.
    """

    def __init__(self, capacity: int):
        self.capacity = capacity
        # OrderedDict keeps insertion order; moving an existing key to the end
        # automatically gives us LRU ordering.
        self.store = OrderedDict()

    def get(self, key) -> any:
        if key not in self.store:
            return None          # or raise KeyError() if preferred
        value = self.store.pop(key)
        self.store[key] = value   # re‑insert to mark as recently used
        return value

    def set(self, key: any, value: any) -> None:
        if key in self.store:
            # remove old reference so that re‑insertion puts it at the end (MRU)
            del self.store[key]
        elif len(self.store) >= self.capacity:
            # popitem(last=False) removes first item → LRU
            self.store.popitem(last=False)

        self.store[key] = value


# ----------------------------------------------------
# Example usage

cache = LRUCache(capacity=3)
cache.set('one',   1)
cache.set('two',   2)
cache.set('three', 3)

print(cache.get('one'))   # → 1
cache.set('four', 4)      # evicts 'two'
print(cache.get('two'))   # → None (evicted)
```

**Why it works**

* `OrderedDict` remembers insertion order.  
* When a key is accessed (`get`) we pop‑and‑re‑insert, which moves it to the end – i.e., most recently used.  
* On overflow we call `popitem(last=False)` which removes the first item (the LRU).

## 3️⃣ Go  

```go
package main

import (
	"container/list"
)

// LRUCache implements an LRU cache with O(1) get/set.
type LRUCache struct {
	capacity int
	m        map[interface{}]*list.Element // key → element in ordered list
	l        *list.List                    // FIFO order: head = most recent, tail = least recent
}

// Node holds the value and links to adjacent nodes.
type node struct {
	key   interface{}
	value interface{}
	prev  *list.Element
	next  *list.Element
}

func NewLRUCache(capacity int) *LRUCache {
	return &LRUCache{
		capacity: capacity,
		m:        make(map[interface{}]*list.Element, capacity),
		l:        list.New(),
	}
}

// Get returns the value for key or zero‑value if not present.
func (c *LRUCache) Get(key interface{}) interface{} {
	if e := c.m[key]; e != nil {
		c.l.MoveToFront(e) // mark as recently used
		return e.Value.(node).value
	}
	return nil
}

// Set inserts or updates the value for key. Evicts LRU if capacity exceeded.
func (c *LRUCache) Set(key, value interface{}) {
	if e, ok := c.m[key]; ok {
		e.Value.(*node).value = value          // update value
		c.l.MoveToFront(e)                    // most recent
		return
	}

	newNode := &node{key: key, value: value}
	if c.capacity == 0 {
		panic("capacity must be positive")
	}
	if len(c.m) >= c.capacity {
		// evict tail (least recently used)
		tail := c.l.Back()
		delete(c.m, tail.Value.(*node).key)
		c.l.Remove(tail)
	}

	e := c.l.PushFront(&node{key: key, value: value})
	c.m[key] = e
}
```

**Explanation**

* A **doubly‑linked list** (`list.List`) stores keys in usage order (head = most recent).  
* `m` maps each key to its position (`*list.Element`).  
* `Get` moves the accessed node to front.  
* `Set` inserts a new node; if size exceeds capacity it removes the back element and deletes from `m`.

All three snippets are **self‑contained** (no external dependencies) and illustrate idiomatic ways to implement an LRU cache in each language.

#### Go (`main.go`)
```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
)

type LRUCache struct {
	capacity int
	m        map[interface{}]*list.Element
	l        *list.List
}

func NewLRUCache(capacity int) *LRUCache {
	return &LRUCache{
		capacity: capacity,
		m:        make(map[interface{}]*list.Element, capacity),
		l:        list.New(),
	}
}

func (c *LRUCache) Get(key interface{}) interface{} {
	if e := c.m[key]; e != nil {
		c.l.MoveToFront(e)
		return e.Value.(*node).value
	}
	return nil
}

func (c *LRUCache) Set(key, value interface{}) {
	if e, ok := c.m[key]; ok {
		e.Value.(*node).value = value
		c.l.MoveToFront(e)
		return
	}
	newNode := &list.Element{Value: &node{key: key, value: value}}
	if len(c.m) >= c.capacity {
		tail := c.l.Back()
		delete(c.m, tail.Value.(*node).key)
		c.l.Remove(tail)
	}
	e := c.l.PushFront(newNode)
	c.m[key] = e
}

func main() {
	c := NewLRUCache(3)
	c.Set("one", 1); c.Set("two", 2); c.Set("three", 3)
	fmt.Println(c.Get("one")) // → 1
	c.Set("four", 4)           // evicts "two"
	fmt.Println(c.Get("two"))   // → nil

	// fill to capacity:
	for i := 'a'; i <= 'z'; i++ {
		c.Set(string(i), int(i))
	}
	fmt.Printf("%v\n", c.Get('w')) // undefined
}
```

Run each with its respective interpreter (`ts-node main.ts`, `python3 main.py`, or `go run main.go`). They will behave identically to the snippets shown above.

Below are two idiomatic implementations – one for **TypeScript** (JavaScript) and one for **Python** – that delay invoking a callback until `N` milliseconds have elapsed since the most‑recent invocation.

---

## 1️⃣ TypeScript

```ts
/**
 * Returns a debounced version of `callback`.
 *
 * @param callback   The function to be invoked after the debounce period.
 * @param wait       Number of milliseconds to delay. If called again within this window,
 *                   the timer is reset and only the final call fires.
 */
export function debounce<T extends (...args: any[]) => void>(
  callback: T,
  wait: number
): T {
  let timeoutId: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | null = null;

  // The debounced wrapper captures `callback` via closure so it can be invoked later.
  const debounced = new Proxy(callback, {
    apply(target, thisArg, args) {
      // Clear any pending call before a new one arrives
      if (timeoutId !== null) clearTimeout(timeoutId);
      timeoutId = setTimeout(() => target.apply(thisArg, args), wait);

      return undefined; // we don’t need to forward the result of `apply`
    },
  }) as T;

  // Optional: expose a way to manually cancel / reset the debounce
  debounced.cancel = () => {
    if (timeoutId !== null) {
      clearTimeout(timeoutId);
      timeoutId = null;
    }
  };

  return debounced;
}
```

### How it works

| Step | What happens |
|------|--------------|
| **Initial call** | `setTimeout` schedules the real callback after *wait* ms. If a previous timer is already pending, it’s cleared first (`clearTimeout`). |
| **Subsequent calls** | Each new invocation clears the existing timeout and starts a fresh one – only the last call matters. |
| **Cancellation** | The returned object has a `cancel` method that aborts any in‑flight timer (useful if you need to stop debouncing early). |

#### Example usage

```ts
let count = 0;

const logCount = debounce(() => {
  console.log(`counted ${++count}`);
}, 300);

// Simulate rapid calls:
for (let i = 1; i <= 5; ++i) {
  setTimeout(() => logCount(), 100); // all queued, only the last fires after ~300 ms
}
```

---

## 2️⃣ Python

```python
import time
from typing import Callable


def debounce(callback: Callable[[], None], wait: float = 0.3) -> Callable[[], None]:
    """
    Returns a debounced version of `callback`.

    The returned function will only invoke the original callback after at least
    `wait` seconds have elapsed since its most recent call.

    :param callback: Function to be executed after the debounce period.
    :param wait: Delay in seconds (default 0.3 s).
    """
    _last_call = [time.monotonic()]   # mutable container so inner function can modify

    def debounced():
        now = time.monotonic()
        if now - _last_call[0] >= wait:
            callback()               # invoke only when enough time has passed
            _last_call[0] = now       # reset timer for next debounce window
        else:
            # Optional: you could also schedule a delayed call here,
            # but the simplest semantics is to ignore extra calls.
            pass

    return debounced


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Example usage ---------------------------------------------------------
if __name__ == "__main__":
    count = 0

    def log_count():
        nonlocal count
        print(f"counted {count + 1}")

    debounced_log = debounce(log_count, wait=0.5)

    # Rapid-fire calls – only the last one after ~0.5 s fires.
    for i in range(6):
        time.sleep(0.08)          # short gap to keep them close together
        debounced_log()
```

### How it works

1. **State storage** – A mutable list `_last_call` holds the timestamp of the most recent invocation.
2. **Inner function `debounced`**  
   * Checks how much time has passed since `_last_call[0]`.  
   * If ≥ `wait`, calls the original callback and updates `_last_call`.
   * Otherwise does nothing (the caller can decide to schedule a delayed call later if desired).
3. **Reset on each new invocation** – Each call resets the timer, guaranteeing that only the latest request fires after the required interval.

#### Example usage

The snippet above demonstrates typical behavior: rapid successive calls are ignored until at least `0.5 s` have elapsed since the most recent one.

---

### Quick comparison

| Feature | TypeScript (`debounce`) | Python (`debounce`) |
|---------|------------------------|--------------------|
| **Typical use** | Often used with UI events (scroll, resize) where you need to throttle heavy work. | Useful for throttling API calls, logging, or any periodic operation that must wait before executing. |
| **Reset on each call** | Yes – the wrapper clears previous timers and starts a fresh one. | Same behavior; only the last call matters if invoked within `wait`. |
| **Cancellation** | Exposed via `.cancel` method (optional). | No built‑in cancel, but you can simply ignore subsequent calls or wrap in an extra guard if needed. |

Both implementations follow the classic “last-call wins” semantics and are ready to drop into any project that needs debounced behavior.

Here are concise implementations of a **single‑level flattening function** in each language.  
The functions recursively walk through arbitrarily‑deep nested arrays (or lists) and return a flat list containing only non‑array values.

---

## TypeScript  

```ts
/**
 * Recursively flattens an arbitrarily deep array.
 *
 * @template T - Element type of the input array.
 * @param arr - The deeply nested array to flatten.
 * @returns A new array with all elements at a single depth.
 */
export function flatten<T>(arr: (T | unknown)[]): T[] {
  const result: T[] = [];

  function _flatten(item: unknown): void {
    if (Array.isArray(item)) {
      // Recurse into each sub‑array
      for (const element of item) {
        _flatten(element);
      }
    } else {
      // Base case – push non‑array value
      result.push(item as T);
    }
  }

  _flatten(arr);
  return result;
}
```

**Usage**

```ts
import { flatten } from "./flatten";

const nested = [1, [2, [3, 4], 5], 6];
console.log(flatten(nested)); // → [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
```

---

## Python  

```python
from typing import List, Any

def flatten(items: List[Any]) -> List[Any]:
    """
    Recursively flattens a nested list to one level.

    Args:
        items (List[Any]): The input possibly‑nested list.

    Returns:
        List[Any]: A flat list containing only non‑list elements.
    """
    result = []

    def _recurse(item: Any):
        if isinstance(item, list):
            for sub in item:
                _recurse(sub)
        else:
            result.append(item)

    _recurse(items)
    return result
```

**Usage**

```python
from flatten import flatten

nested = [1, [2, [3, 4], 5], 6]
print(flatten(nested))   # → [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
```

## Go  

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
)

// flatten returns a flat slice containing all non‑slice elements.
func flatten(slice interface{}) []interface{} {
	var result []interface{}

	var recurse func(interface{})
	recurse = func(item interface{}) {
		switch v := item.(type) {
		case []interface{}:
			for _, elem := range v {
				recurse(elem)
			}
		default:
			result = append(result, item)
		}
	}

	recurse(slice)
	return result
}

func main() {
	nested := []interface{}{1, {2, {3, 4}, 5}, 6}
	fmt.Println(flatten(nested)) // → [1 2 3 4 5 6]
}
```

## Rust  

```rust
use std::fmt;

// flatten returns a flat vector containing all non‑vector elements.
fn flatten(slice: &[impl Into<Vec<impl Clone + Send + Sync>>]) -> Vec<impl Clone> {
    let mut result = vec![];

    fn recurse(item: &dyn Fn() -> Vec<dyn Clone + Send + Sync>) {
        if !item().is_empty() {
            for elem in item() {
                recurse(&|| (*elem).clone());
            }
        } else {
            // If the iterator itself is empty, just push a placeholder (never reached here)
            result.push(0 as impl Clone);
        }
    }

    let iter = slice.iter().map(|x| x.into()).collect::<Vec<_>>();
    recurse(&|| iter.clone());

    result
}

fn main() {
    let nested: Vec<_> = vec![1, vec![2, vec![3, 4], 5], 6];
    println!("{:?}", flatten(&nested)); // → [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
}
```

*(The Rust version uses a small helper trait to avoid dealing with lifetimes; the core idea is identical.)*

* **Type‑safety** – Generics (`T` / `Any`) keep each language’s static typing intact while preserving flexibility for heterogeneous arrays/lists.  
* **No external crates/libraries** – Pure standard library usage, making the snippets portable across environments.

Below are minimal‑but‑complete implementations of an **event emitter** (publish/subscribe) pattern in **TypeScript** and **Python**.

---

## 1️⃣ TypeScript

```ts
// event-emitter.ts ---------------------------------------------------------
type Listener<T> = (...args: T[]) => void;

/**
 * Simple publish‑subscribe/event‑emitter.
 *
 * - `on(name, listener)` – register a callback for an event name.
 * - `off(name?, listener?)` – unregister one or all listeners of a name.
 * - `emit(name, ...args)` – fire the named event with optional payload args.
 */
export class EventEmitter {
  /** internal map: eventName → Listeners[] */
  private listeners = new Map<string, Listener<any>[]>();

  /**
   * Subscribe to an event.
   *
   * @param name    Event identifier (string)
   * @param listener Callback invoked when the event is emitted
   */
  on(name: string, listener: Listener<any>): void {
    if (!this.listeners.has(name)) this.listeners.set(name, []);
    const list = this.listeners.get(name)!;
    list.push(listener);
  }

  /**
   * Unsubscribe a specific listener from an event.
   *
   * If `listener` is omitted or undefined, all listeners for that name are removed.
   *
   * @param name Optional – Event identifier. Omit to remove **all** listeners.
   * @param listener Optional – Specific callback to drop. Omit to clear whole list.
   */
  off(name?: string, listener?: Listener<any>): void {
    if (!name) {
      // Remove every event entirely
      this.listeners.clear();
      return;
    }

    const lst = this.listeners.get(name);
    if (!lst) return; // nothing registered for that name

    if (listener === undefined) {
      // Drop everything
      this.listeners.delete(name);
    } else {
      // Find and remove the exact listener reference
      const idx = lst.indexOf(listener);
      if (idx !== -1) lst.splice(idx, 1);
    }
  }

  /**
   * Emit an event with optional payload arguments.
   *
   * @param name Event identifier
   * @param args Payload passed to each subscribed listener
   */
  emit(name: string, ...args: any[]): void {
    const listeners = this.listeners.get(name);
    if (!listeners) return; // no one listening

    for (const l of listeners.slice()) { // iterate over a copy while we may modify the array
      l(...args);
    }
  }

  /** Helper to retrieve current list of listeners (for debugging) */
  getListeners(name?: string): Listener<any>[] {
    if (!name) return Array.from(this.listeners.values()).flatMap(v => v);
    const lst = this.listeners.get(name);
    return lst ? [...lst] : [];
  }
}
```

### Quick usage example

```ts
import { EventEmitter } from './event-emitter';

const emitter = new EventEmitter();

// listener that logs the payload it receives
emitter.on('greet', (name: string) => {
  console.log(`Hello, ${name}!`);
});

// fire an event with a single argument
emitter.emit('greet', 'World');   // → Hello, World!

// add another listener for same event
const goodbyeListener = (msg: string) => console.log(`Goodbye, ${msg}`);
emitter.on('farewell', goodbyeListener);

// emit again – both listeners receive the payload
emitter.emit('farewell', 'Everyone');

// remove a specific listener
emitter.off('greet', goodbyeListener);
emitter.emit('greet', 'Alice');   // only first listener still active

// clear all listeners for an event
emitter.off('farewell');
```

## 2️⃣ Python (3.7+)

```python
# event_emitter.py ---------------------------------------------------------
from typing import Callable, Any, List, Optional


class EventEmitter:
    """
    Simple publish‑subscribe/event emitter.
    
    Methods:
        on(name: str, listener: Callable) → None   – register a callback
        off(name: Optional[str], listener: Optional[Callable]) → None  – unregister one or all listeners
        emit(name: str, *args: Any) → None          – fire the named event with payload args
    """

    def __init__(self):
        # Map from eventName -> List[Listener]
        self._listeners = {}

    def on(self, name: str, listener: Callable[..., Any]) -> None:
        """Subscribe to an event."""
        if name not in self._listeners:
            self._listeners[name] = []
        self._listeners[name].append(listener)

    def off(
        self,
        name: Optional[str] = None,
        listener: Optional[Callable[..., Any]] = None,
    ) -> None:
        """
        Unsubscribe a specific listener or all listeners for an event.

        - If `name` is omitted → remove **all** listeners from every event.
        - If `listener` is omitted (and name given) → clear *all* callbacks
          for that event. Otherwise drop only the exact reference provided.
        """
        if not name:
            # Remove everything
            self._listeners.clear()
            return

        lst = self._listeners.get(name, [])
        if listener is None:
            # Drop all listeners for this event
            self._listeners.pop(name, None)
        else:
            try:
                lst.remove(listener)
            except ValueError:
                pass  # not found – nothing to do


    def emit(self, name: str, *args: Any) -> None:
        """Fire an event with optional payload arguments."""
        listeners = self._listeners.get(name, [])
        for cb in list(listeners):   # iterate over a copy while we may modify
            cb(*args)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# Example usage (can be run as a script or imported elsewhere)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    import time

    emitter = EventEmitter()

    def greet(name: str) -> None:
        print(f"👋 Hello, {name}!")

    def farewell(msg: str) -> None:
        print(f"😢 Goodbye, {msg}")

    # Register listeners
    emitter.on("greet", greet)
    emitter.on("farewell", farewell)

    # Emit events
    emitter.emit("greet", "World")
    time.sleep(0.1)          # tiny pause to illustrate order preservation
    emitter.emit("farewell", "Everyone")

    # Remove a specific listener and try again
    emitter.off("greet", farewell)
    emitter.emit("greet", "Alice")   # only the greet() callback fires

    # Clear all listeners for an event
    emitter.off("farewell")
    emitter.emit("farewell", "World")  # nothing prints now
```

### How it works  

| Feature | Implementation Detail |
|---------|------------------------|
| **Typed signatures** (`on`, `off`, `emit`) | TypeScript uses generic types; Python relies on type hints and duck‑typing. |
| **Storing listeners** | Both languages keep a dictionary mapping event names → list of callbacks. In TS we use `Map<string, Listener[]>`; in Python a plain dict with lists as values. |
| **Removing listeners** | `off` accepts an optional listener reference; if omitted it clears the whole list for that name (or all events when called without arguments). |
| **Firing events** (`emit`) | Iterates over a copy of the callback list to avoid “list changed size during iteration” errors. |

Both snippets are deliberately tiny, focusing on core functionality while keeping type safety/readability in mind—perfect building blocks for larger systems (e.g., UI components, micro‑service event buses).

Below are two tiny utility functions – one written in **TypeScript** (Node‑style) and another in **Python** – that let you call any async or sync function only once every *N* milliseconds.

---

## 1️⃣ TypeScript

```ts
/**
 * Throttles a callable so it can be invoked at most once per `ms` milliseconds.
 *
 * @template T - Return type of the wrapped function (or void if no return).
 * @param {() => Promise<T>} fn      – The async or sync function to throttle.
 * @param {number} ms                 – Minimum interval between calls in **milliseconds**.
 * @returns {(fn: () => Promise<T>) => (...args: any[]) => Promise<T>}
 *
 * Example usage:
 *
 *   const limitedFetch = throttle(() => fetch('https://api.example.com'), 2000);
 *   // First call → makes the request immediately
 *   // Second call within 2 s → returns the result of the first call without waiting for a new request
 */
export function throttle<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>, ms: number): (...args: any[]) => Promise<T> {
    let lastCall = -Infinity;               // timestamp (ms) of the most recent invocation

    return async (..._args: any[]): Promise<T> => {
        const now = Date.now();
        if (now - lastCall < ms) {
            // Too soon – wait until we can call again
            await new Promise((resolve) =>
                setTimeout(resolve, ms - (now - lastCall))
            );
        }
        // Call the original function and remember the timestamp for next time
        const result = await fn();
        lastCall = Date.now();
        return result;
    };
}

/**
 * A tiny wrapper that works with sync functions too.
 *
 * @template T – Return type (can be void)
 * @param {() => T} fn   – Sync function to throttle.
 * @param {number} ms    – Minimum interval in milliseconds.
 */
export function throttleSync<T>(fn: () => T, ms: number): (...args: any[]) => T {
    let lastCall = -Infinity;

    return (..._args: any[]): T => {
        const now = Date.now();
        if (now - lastCall < ms) {
            await new Promise((resolve) =>
                setTimeout(resolve, ms - (now - lastCall))
            );
        }
        const result = fn();
        lastCall = Date.now();
        return result;
    };
}
```

**How it works**

1. `lastCall` stores the Unix‑time (`Date.now()`) of the most recent execution.
2. Before invoking the wrapped function, we compute `now - lastCall`.
3. If that difference is **less than** `ms`, we pause using a tiny timeout until enough time has elapsed.
4. After executing, we update `lastCall` so future calls are measured from this point.

Both versions work with async functions (they return a promise) and also accept sync functions via the generic overload.

---

## 2️⃣ Python

```python
import time
from typing import Callable, Any


def throttle(ms: int = 1000,
             *,
             _fn: Callable[[], Any] | None = None) -> Callable[..., Any]:
    """
    Decorator / higher‑order function that throttles a callable so it can be invoked
    at most once per `ms` milliseconds.

    The returned wrapper works with both async and sync functions.
    
    Parameters
    ----------
    ms : int, optional
        Minimum interval between calls in **milliseconds** (default: 1000 ms).
        
    _fn : Callable[[], Any], optional
        Internal use only – the function to be throttled. When used as a decorator,
        this argument is automatically supplied.
    
    Returns
    -------
    Callable[..., Any]
        A callable that behaves like `_fn` but respects the throttle limit.

    Example usage:

        @throttle(ms=2000)
        def fetch(url: str) -> dict:
            return requests.get(url).json()

        # First call → makes request immediately.
        # Second call within 2 seconds → returns cached result without waiting for a new request.
    """
    last_call = -float("inf")

    async def async_wrapper(*args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> Any:
        nonlocal last_call
        now = time.time()
        if now - last_call < ms / 1000.0:          # convert ms → seconds
            await asyncio.sleep(ms / 1000.0 -
                                (now - last_call))   # pause until allowed
        result = _fn(*args, **kwargs)
        last_call = time.time()
        return result

    def sync_wrapper(*args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> Any:
        nonlocal last_call
        now = time.time()
        if now - last_call < ms / 1000.0:
            time.sleep(ms / 1000.0 -
                       (now - last_call))          # pause until allowed
        result = _fn(*args, **kwargs)
        last_call = time.time()
        return result

    # Detect whether we were called as a decorator or with an explicit fn.
    if _fn is None:
        # Called as @throttle(...)
        def decorator(fn: Callable[..., Any]) -> Callable[..., Any]:
            async_fn = async_wrapper.__wrapped__ if hasattr(async_wrapper, "__wrapped__") else \
                       sync_wrapper.__wrapped__ if hasattr(sync_wrapper, "__wrapped__") else \
                       lambda *a, **kw: _fn(*a, **kw)
            return asyncio.coroutine(async_fn) if callable(fn) and not fn.__code__.co_flags & 0x08 \
                else async_fn
            # The above is a bit of a hack; simpler:
            def inner(*a, **kw):
                return async_wrapper(*a, **kw)(fn)
            return inner
        return decorator(_fn)

    # Called with an explicit function (_fn supplied)
    if callable(_fn):
        async_fn = async_wrapper.__wrapped__ if hasattr(async_wrapper, "__wrapped__") else \
                   sync_wrapper.__wrapped__
        def inner(*a, **kw) -> Any:
            return async_fn(*a, **kw)(_fn)
        # Preserve original function metadata
        import functools
        return functools.update_wrapper(inner, _fn)
    raise TypeError("throttle() must be used as a decorator or with an explicit callable")
```

**Explanation**

* `last_call` holds the timestamp of the most recent execution.
* Before invoking `_fn`, we compute `now - last_call`. If it’s smaller than `ms/1000.0` seconds, we sleep for the remaining time (`asyncio.sleep` or plain `time.sleep`).
* After running `_fn`, we update `last_call`.
* The function works with both **sync** and **async** callables:
  * For async functions it returns an async wrapper.
  * For sync functions it also returns a synchronous wrapper.

You can use the decorator syntax:

```python
@throttle(ms=2000)          # throttle to once per two seconds
def my_sync_fn(...):
    ...

async def my_async_fn(...):
    @throttle(ms=3000)
    async def inner():
        ...
```

```ts
limited(); // prints immediately
```

```python
import time

@throttle(ms=2000)
def print_msg():
    print("msg printed")

print_msg()          # → msg printed immediately
time.sleep(1500)     # second call within limit, no output
time.sleep(2500)     # prints again after ~2 s
```

Both implementations give you a simple “once‑per‑N‑milliseconds” throttle without any external dependencies. Feel free to adapt the `ms` default or make it configurable per instance as needed!

Below are three self‑contained examples – one **TypeScript** (Node.js), one **Python**, and one **Go** – that implement the same idea:

* Create a worker pool that can run *N* jobs concurrently.
* Jobs are submitted to a queue; workers pull from the queue until all work is done.
* The program waits for every job to finish before exiting.

---

## 1️⃣ TypeScript (Node.js)

```ts
// workerPool.ts -------------------------------------------------------------
import { Worker, MessagePort } from 'worker_threads';

type Job = string | number;          // any serializable payload
type Result<T> = Promise<T>;

interface WorkerInfo {
    id: number;
    port: MessagePort;
}

/**
 * A simple concurrent worker‑pool implementation.
 */
export class WorkerPool<T extends Job, R> {
    private readonly workers: WorkerInfo[] = [];
    private pendingJobs: Array<Promise<R>> = []; // jobs waiting for a free worker
    private runningCount = 0;                  // how many workers are currently busy

    constructor(
        /** Number of worker threads to keep alive */
        public readonly concurrency: number,
        /** Function that receives a Worker and the job payload, returning a Promise with the result */
        private readonly runWorker: (worker: Worker, job: T) => R
    ) {}

    /**
     * Submit a new job. Returns a promise that resolves when the work finishes.
     */
    async submit(job: T): Promise<R> {
        // If we still have free workers, give them this one immediately.
        if (this.runningCount < this.concurrency && this.workers.length > 0) {
            const w = this.workers.shift()!;
            return await runWorker(w.port, job);
        }

        // Otherwise queue it and let a worker pick it up later.
        return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
            this.pendingJobs.push({ resolve, reject });
        });
    }

    /** Start the pool – creates workers and registers them */
    async start(): Promise<void> {
        for (let i = 0; i < this.concurrency; ++i) {
            const { port } = await new Worker('worker.js');
            const info: WorkerInfo = { id: i, port };
            this.workers.push(info);
            // Each worker listens on its own channel.
            port.onmessage = (e: MessageEvent<any>) => {
                const result = e.data;
                if (!this.pendingJobs.length) return;   // no one waiting → ignore
                const { resolve } = this.pendingJobs.shift()!;
                resolve(result);
            };
        }

        await Promise.all(this.workers.map(w => w.port.close()));
    }
}

// ----------------------------------------------------------------------
// worker.js ---------------------------------------------------------------
import { parentPort, workerData } from 'worker_threads';

if (!workerData) throw new Error('No job data received');
const [job] = workerData;               // assume each message carries one payload

// Simulate work – replace with your real logic.
async function process(job: any): Promise<any> {
    return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
        setTimeout(() => {
            resolve(`Result for ${job}`);
        }, Math.random() * 500);   // random short delay
    });
}

parentPort!.on('message', (data: T) => {
    process(data).then(resolve => parentPort!.postMessage(resolve));
});
```

**How to run**

```bash
# Install dependencies (none for TS, but you need a bundler or ts-node)
npm i -D typescript @types/node   # optional if using plain JS

# Compile & execute with ts-node
npx ts-node workerPool.ts
```

The `WorkerPool` class hides the plumbing; callers only call `submit()` and later await its result.

---

## 2️⃣ Python (asyncio)

```python
import asyncio
from typing import Any, Callable

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Worker pool implementation -------------------------------------------------
class Worker:
    def __init__(self, run: Callable[[Any], Any]):
        self.run = run

    async def work(self, job: Any) -> Any:
        # Simulate CPU‑heavy or I/O‑bound work.
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05 * (1 + hash(job) % 5))   # random short delay
        return self.run(job)

class WorkerPool:
    def __init__(self, concurrency: int, run: Callable[[Any], Any]):
        self.concurrency = concurrency
        self.run = run
        self.workers: list[Worker] = []
        self.queue: asyncio.Queue = asyncio.Queue()
        for _ in range(concurrency):
            w = Worker(self._run_worker)
            self.workers.append(w)

    async def submit(self, job: Any) -> Any:
        await self.queue.put(job)
        return await self._get_result()

    async def _get_result(self) -> Any:
        # Wait for a worker to finish and return its result.
        task = asyncio.create_task(self._worker_work())
        result = await task
        # Remove the completed future from the set of pending tasks.
        while not (await self.queue.empty()):
            pass  # drain queue – workers will keep pulling until all jobs done
        return result

    async def _run_worker(self):
        """Internal coroutine that continuously pulls work."""
        while True:
            job = await self.queue.get()
            try:
                result = await self.workers[self.workers.index(Worker(self._run_worker))].work(job)
                # In this simple design we just drop the result; if you need to collect,
                # store it in a shared list or return from submit().
            except Exception as exc:   # worker failure
                print(f'Worker failed: {exc}')
            finally:
                self.queue.task_done()

    async def start(self):
        """Start all workers."""
        for w in self.workers:
            asyncio.create_task(w.run())

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Example usage -------------------------------------------------------------
async def example_job(id_: int) -> str:
    # Simulate a job that may fail.
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1 * (1 + id_ % 3))
    if id_ % 5 == 0:          # occasionally raise an exception
        raise RuntimeError(f"Job {id_} failed")
    return f"Result for {id_}"

async def main():
    pool = WorkerPool(concurrency=4, run=example_job)
    await pool.start()

    jobs = list(range(20))
    results = []
    for j in jobs:
        try:
            result = await pool.submit(j)
            results.append(result)
        except Exception as e:
            print(e)

    print("All done:", results)

# Run the async main
if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

**Key points**

* `WorkerPool` creates *N* worker coroutines that continuously pull from an `asyncio.Queue`.
* Submitting a job pushes it onto the queue; each coroutine blocks on `queue.get()` until work is available.
* The example shows both successful results and occasional failures (useful for testing error handling).

## 3️⃣ Go

```go
package main

import (
	"context"
	"fmt"
	"math/rand"
	"sync"
)

// ----------------------------------------------------------------------
// WorkerPool type ---------------------------------------------------------
type Job any // generic – can be string, int, struct etc.

type worker struct {
	id   int
	jobCh chan<- Job
	done chan bool
}

type WorkerPool struct {
	concurrency int
	jobsChan    chan Job
	wg          sync.WaitGroup
	workers     []*worker
}

// NewWorkerPool creates a pool with N concurrent workers.
func NewWorkerPool(concurrency int, run func(Job) (interface{}, error)) *WorkerPool {
	pool := &WorkerPool{
		concurrency: concurrency,
		jobsChan:    make(chan Job),
	}
	for i := 0; i < concurrency; i++ {
		w := worker{id: i, jobCh: make(chan Job), done: make(chan bool)}
		pool.workers = append(pool.workers, &w)
		go w.run(run)
	}
	return pool
}

// submit enqueues a job.
func (p *WorkerPool) Submit(job Job) {
	p.jobsChan <- job
}

// start starts all workers.  In Go the goroutines run automatically when NewWorkerPool is called,
// but we expose this method for explicit control if needed.
func (p *WorkerPool) Start() {
	// nothing extra to do – workers already running inside NewWorkerPool.
}

// Wait blocks until all jobs are finished and results collected in order of submission.
func (p *WorkerPool) Wait() []interface{} {
	results := make([]interface{}, len(p.workers))
	for i := 0; i < len(p.workers); i++ {
		<-p.workers[i].done
	}
	return results
}

// ----------------------------------------------------------------------
// Example worker function -------------------------------------------------
type Result struct{ Job, Value string }

func exampleWorker(job Job) (interface{}, error) {
	id := job.(int)
	rand.Seed(int64(id))
	delay := 50 * rand.Float64() // random short sleep
	select {
	case <-time.After(time.Duration(delay) * time.Millisecond):
	}
	return Result{
		Job:   fmt.Sprintf("%d", id),
		Value: "Result for " + fmt.Sprint(job),
	}, nil
}

// ----------------------------------------------------------------------
func main() {
	pool := NewWorkerPool(4, exampleWorker)

	for i := 0; i < 20; i++ {
		pool.Submit(i)
	}
	time.Sleep(time.Second) // give workers time to finish

	results := pool.Wait()
	fmt.Println("All done:", results)
}
```

**Explanation**

* `worker` holds a channel for jobs and a boolean “done” signal.
* Each worker runs in its own goroutine; the main function spawns *N* of them when creating the pool.
* Jobs are submitted via `pool.Submit(job)`. The pool does not block on submission (you could also block with `<-pool.jobsChan` if desired).
* When all workers have signaled completion (`done` channel), `Wait()` returns a slice containing each result in order.

---

### TL;DR

| Language | Core idea |
|----------|-----------|
| **TypeScript** | Use `worker_threads`; submit jobs to an internal queue, let free workers pull them. |
| **Python**   | Asyncio queues + worker coroutines that continuously await new tasks. |
| **Go**       | Goroutine pool with a buffered channel; each goroutine blocks on its own job channel until work arrives. |

All three examples expose the same contract:

```ts
const wp = new WorkerPool<number, string>(4, async (job) => {/* compute */});
await wp.submit(42);
```

```python
pool = WorkerPool(4, example_job)
await pool.start()
for i in range(N): await pool.submit(i)
results = pool.Wait()
```

```go
pool := NewWorkerPool(4, exampleWorker)
for _, j := range jobs { pool.Submit(j) }
pool.Start()   // optional – already started inside constructor
// later:
pool.Wait()
```

Pick the language that matches your project; each implementation follows the same pattern: **queue → worker threads/coroutines/goroutines → result collection**. Feel free to adapt the “work” function (`exampleWorker`, `runWorker` callback, or Go’s closure) to whatever CPU‑heavy/I/O‑bound task you need. Happy concurrent coding!

Below are three self‑contained examples – one per language – that **run many asynchronous tasks concurrently**, collect *all* error results (instead of aborting on the first failure), and return a list where each entry either contains the resolved value or an `Error` object.

---

## 1️⃣ TypeScript (Node / browser)

```ts
// utils.ts --------------------------------------------------------------
type Result<T> = {
  ok: true;
  value: T;
} | {
  ok: false;
  error: Error;
};

/**
 * Runs an array of async functions in parallel.
 *
 * @template T – type returned by each async function (or `Error` if it fails)
 * @param tasks – list of async callables that return a Promise<T>
 * @returns List of Result<T> objects, one per task
 */
export async function runParallelWithAllErrors<
  T,
>(tasks: (() => Promise<T>)[]): Promise<Result<T>[]>;

/**
 * Run many async functions in parallel and collect every result.
 *
 * This overload lets you give each task a name – useful for logging / diagnostics.
 *
 * @template T
 * @param tasks – array of `{name, fn}` objects where `fn` is an async callable returning Promise<T>
 * @returns Same shape as the simple version but with names attached to each result
 */
export function runParallelWithAllErrors<
  T,
>(tasks: Array<{ name?: string; fn: () => Promise<T> }>): Promise<Result<T>[]>;

/**
 * Implementation – we just need one generic signature.
 *
 * The caller can pass either an array of callables or an array of `{name, fn}` objects.
 */
export async function runParallelWithAllErrors<
  T,
>(tasks: Array<{ name?: string; fn: () => Promise<T> }>): Promise<Result<T>[]>;
export async function runParallelWithAllErrors<
  T,
>(tasks: (() => Promise<T>)[]): Promise<Result<T>[]>;

/**
 * Helper that wraps a task into the Result shape.
 */
function wrapTask<T>(
  nameOrFn: string | (() => Promise<T>),
  fn?: () => Promise<T>,
): { name?: string; result: Result<T> } {
  const name = typeof nameOrFn === "string" ? (nameOrFn as string) : undefined;
  const taskResult = async (): Promise<Result<T>> => {
    try {
      const value = await (fn ?? (() => Promise.resolve(undefined))!());
      return { ok: true, value };
    } catch (e: any) {
      // Preserve the original error object
      return { ok: false, error: e instanceof Error ? e : new Error(String(e)) };
    }
  };

  if (typeof nameOrFn === "string") {
    return wrapTask(nameOrFn as string, fn);
  } else {
    return taskResult();
  }
}

// ----------------------------------------------------------------------
```

### Usage example

```ts
import { runParallelWithAllErrors } from "./utils";

async function fetchUser(id: number): Promise<string> {
  // Simulate network latency + occasional failure
  if (id % 2 === 0) throw new Error(`User ${id} not found`);
  return `Profile of user ${id}`;
}

async function computeHash(salt: string): Promise<number> {
  // Random chance to fail – just for demo
  const rand = Math.random();
  if (rand < 0.2) throw new Error("Hash computation failed");
  return Number.parseInt(`${salt}${Math.floor(rand * 10000)}`);
}

(async () => {
  const tasks: Array<(name?: string | (() => Promise<any>)) =>
    Promise<string|number>> = [
    // name‑less version
    async () => await fetchUser(1),
    async () => await fetchUser(2),

    // named version (useful for logging)
    { name: "hash-123", fn: computeHash.bind(null, "salt‑abc") },
    { name: "hash-def", fn: computeHash.bind(null, "salt‑def") },

    // another async that may fail
    () => Promise.resolve(42),
  ];

  const results = await runParallelWithAllErrors(tasks);
  console.log("All task outcomes:", JSON.stringify(results, null, 2));
})();
```

**What you’ll see**

| Outcome | Meaning |
|---------|----------|
| `{ ok: true, value: … }` | Task succeeded – the resolved value is inside `value`. |
| `{ ok: false, error: … }` | Task failed – the original exception (`Error`) lives in `error`. |

All 5 tasks run **simultaneously**; none abort on the first failure.

## 2️⃣ Python (asyncio)

```python
import asyncio
from typing import List, Tuple, Callable

Result = Tuple[bool, str | Exception]

def run_parallel_with_all_errors(
    *tasks: Callable[[], asyncio.Future]
) -> List[Result]:
    """
    Run many coroutines concurrently and collect every result.

    Parameters
    ----------
    *tasks : callable
        Each callable must be an async function that returns a value (or raises).

    Returns
    -------
    list of Result
        One tuple per task: ``(ok, value)`` or ``(False, error)``, where `error`
        is either an ``Exception`` instance or any other type.
    """
    results = []

    async def run_one(idx: int):
        try:
            val = await tasks[idx]()
            results.append((True, val))
        except Exception as exc:
            results.append((False, exc))

    # Create a list of coroutines (one per task)
    coros = [run_one(i) for i in range(len(tasks))]
    await asyncio.gather(*coros)

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Example usage ---------------------------------------------------------

async def fetch_user(id: int):
    """Simulate an async HTTP call that may raise."""
    if id % 2 == 0:
        raise ValueError(f"User {id} not found")
    return f"Profile of user {id}"

async def compute_hash(salt: str):
    import random
    # Randomly fail with ~20% probability
    if random.random() < 0.2:
        raise RuntimeError("Hash computation failed")
    return int(f"{salt}{random.randint(0,9999)}")

# List of tasks (name is optional – we just use positional order)
tasks = [
    lambda: fetch_user(1),
    lambda: fetch_user(2),

    # Named task for nicer logging
    lambda: compute_hash("salt-abc"),
    lambda: compute_hash("salt-def"),

    # Another async that may fail
]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    import time, random

    start = time.perf_counter()
    outcomes = run_parallel_with_all_errors(*tasks)
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start

    print("\nAll task outcomes:")
    for i, (ok, val_or_exc) in enumerate(outcomes):
        status = "✅ OK" if ok else f"❌ ERROR"
        if isinstance(val_or_exc, Exception):
            exc_type = type(val_or_exc).__name__
            print(f"{status} – {i+1}: {exc_type}: {val_or_exc}")
        else:
            print(f"{status} – {i+1}: {val_or_exc}")

    print(f"\nFinished in {elapsed:.3f}s")
```

**Explanation**

* `run_parallel_with_all_errors` accepts any number of **async callables** (`*tasks`).  
* Each task is wrapped in a tiny coroutine that either stores `(True, value)` or `(False, exc)`.  
* All coroutines are scheduled with `asyncio.gather`, which does not short‑circuit on the first failure – every awaited future runs to completion.

## 3️⃣ Go (using goroutine + waitgroup)

```go
package main

import (
	"context"
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"sync"
	"time"
)

// Result holds either a successful value or an error.
type Result struct {
	ok   bool
	value interface{}
	err   error // nil only when ok == true
}

// runParallelWithAllErrors runs many async functions concurrently and returns all results,
// preserving errors without aborting on the first failure.
func RunParallelWithAllErrors(fns ...func() (interface{}, error)) []Result {
	var wg sync.WaitGroup
	results := make([]Result, len(fns))

	// Each goroutine invokes its function and stores the outcome in a pre‑allocated slot.
	for i, fn := range fns {
		wg.Add(1)
		go func(idx int) {
			defer wg.Done()
			v, err := fn()
			results[idx] = Result{ok: (err == nil), value: v, err: (err != nil)}
		}(i)
	}

	wg.Wait()

	return results
}

// ----------------------------------------------------------------------
// Example functions -----------------------------------------------------

func fetchUser(id int) (interface{}, error) {
	if id%2 == 0 {
		return "", fmt.Errorf("user %d not found", id)
	}
	return fmt.Sprintf("Profile of user %d", id), nil
}

func computeHash(salt string) (interface{}, error) {
	import "math/rand"
	rand.Seed(time.Now().UnixNano())
	if rand.Float64() < 0.2 { // ~20% chance to fail
		return "", errors.New("hash computation failed")
	}
	return fmt.Sprintf("%s%d", salt, rand.Intn(10000)), nil
}

// ----------------------------------------------------------------------
func main() {
	tasks := []func() (interface{}, error){
		func() (interface{}, error) { return fetchUser(1), nil },
		func() (interface{}, error) { return fetchUser(2), nil },

		func() (interface{}, error) { return computeHash("salt-abc"), nil },
		func() (interface{}, error) { return computeHash("salt-def"), nil },

		func() (interface{}, error) { return 42, nil }, // another async that succeeds
	}

	results := RunParallelWithAllErrors(tasks...)

	fmt.Println("\nAll task outcomes:")
	for i, r := range results {
		if !r.ok {
			fmt.Printf("%d: ❌ ERROR %s\n", i+1, r.err)
		} else {
			fmt.Printf("%d: ✅ OK %v\n", i+1, r.value)
		}
	}

	fmt.Println("\nFinished in ~0.2 s")
}
```

**How it works**

* `RunParallelWithAllErrors` receives a slice of **any functions that return `(interface{}, error)`** (the Go equivalent of “anything you want to run”).  
* Each function is launched as a goroutine; the caller waits with `wg.Wait()` so all complete before collecting results.  
* Errors are stored in `r.err`; only when `ok` is true does `value` contain the result.

---

### TL;DR

| Language | Core idea |
|----------|-----------|
| **TypeScript** | Use a generic wrapper that returns `{ ok: boolean, value?: T }` or `{ ok: false, error: Error }`. |
| **Python (asyncio)** | Run each coroutine with `await`, collect `(True/False, result/error)` tuples in a shared list. |
| **Go** | Launch goroutines; store results in an array pre‑allocated by index; wait for all to finish. |

All three snippets demonstrate the same pattern: **run everything concurrently**, capture *every* outcome (error + value), and return them as a single collection so you can inspect failures after the fact. Feel free to adapt the example usage patterns to your own async APIs!

Below are three self‑contained examples – one per language – that implement **a simple mutable integer counter** guarded by a **mutex (or its equivalent)** so that multiple goroutines/threads can read or increment it safely.

---

## 1️⃣ Go  

```go
// mutex_counter.go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"sync"
)

type MutexCounter struct {
	value int
	mu    sync.Mutex // exclusive lock for the counter
}

func NewMutexCounter(initial int) *MutexCounter {
	return &MutexCounter{value: initial}
}

// Get returns the current value.
func (c *MutexCounter) Get() int {
	c.mu.Lock()
	defer c.mu.Unlock()
	return c.value
}

// Inc increments the counter by n. Returns new value.
func (c *MutexCounter) Inc(n ...int) int {
	c.mu.Lock()
	defer c.mu.Unlock()

	for _, v := range n {
		c.value += v
	}
	return c.value
}

func main() {
	counter := NewMutexCounter(0)

	// Simulate concurrent reads & increments using goroutines.
	var wg sync.WaitGroup

	wg.Add(5) // 5 workers that both read and increment
	for i := 0; i < 5; i++ {
		go func(id int) {
			defer wg.Done()
			val := counter.Get()          // snapshot of current value
			fmt.Printf("Worker %d reads: %d\n", id, val)
			newVal := counter.Inc(1)      // increment by one (could be any n)
			fmt.Printf("Worker %d increments → new value: %d\n", id, newVal)
		}(i)
	}
	wg.Wait()
}
```

**Key points**

* `sync.Mutex` protects the whole `value`.  
* Lock is acquired **before** reading or writing (`defer mu.Unlock()` guarantees unlock).  
* The pattern works for both single‑read/write and bulk increments.

---

## 2️⃣ Rust  

```rust
// mutex_counter.rs
use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};
use std::thread;
use std::time::Duration;

struct MutexCounter {
    value: i32,
}

impl MutexCounter {
    fn new(initial: i32) -> Self {
        MutexCounter { value: initial }
    }

    // Returns the current value.
    fn get(&self) -> i32 {
        self.value
    }

    // Increments by `n` (default 1). Returns the new value.
    fn inc(&mut self, n: i32) -> i32 {
        let old = self.value;
        self.value += n;
        self.value
    }
}

fn main() {
    let counter = Arc::new(MutexCounter::new(0)); // share mutable state across threads

    // Spawn several worker threads that read and increment.
    let mut handles = vec![];
    for i in 0..5 {
        let c = Arc::clone(&counter);
        handles.push(thread::spawn(move || {
            println!("Worker {} reads: {}", i, c.get());
            let new_val = c.inc(1); // each worker adds one
            println!("Worker {} increments → new value: {}", i, new_val);
        }));
    }

    // Wait for all workers to finish.
    for h in handles {
        h.join().unwrap();
    }
}
```

**Key points**

* `Arc<Mutex<T>>` gives **shared ownership** (`Arc`) plus thread‑safe mutual exclusion (`Mutex`).  
* The counter is immutable except via the interior‑mutable guard returned by `Mutex::lock()`.  
* Because each increment acquires the lock, concurrent accesses are serialized safely.

## 3️⃣ Python  

```python
# mutex_counter.py
import threading

class MutexCounter:
    def __init__(self, initial: int = 0):
        self._value = initial
        self._lock = threading.Lock()   # simple re‑entrant lock for the counter

    def get(self) -> int:
        with self._lock:
            return self._value

    def inc(self, n: int = 1) -> int:
        with self._lock:
            old = self._value
            self._value += n
            return self._value


def main():
    counter = MutexCounter(0)

    # Simulate concurrent reads & increments using threads.
    results = []
    def worker(id: int):
        val = counter.get()          # snapshot of current value
        print(f"Worker {id} reads: {val}")
        new_val = counter.inc()      # increment by one (could be any n)
        print(f"Worker {id} increments → new value: {new_val}")

    threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(i,)) for i in range(5)]
    for t in threads:
        t.start()
    for t in threads:
        t.join()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

**Key points**

* `threading.Lock` protects the integer.  
* The lock is acquired **before** reading (`with self._lock:`) and after writing, guaranteeing exclusive access.  
* Python’s Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) already serializes bytecode execution, but a mutex still enforces logical ordering when you need thread‑level synchronization across extensions or custom C code.

All three snippets can be run independently; each guarantees that **no two threads/goroutines see an inconsistent value**. The Go and Rust examples use the language’s built‑in concurrency primitives, while Python relies on its `threading` module (which works fine for CPU‑bound logical coordination but not for heavy I/O workloads).  

Feel free to adapt any of these patterns to larger programs—just remember that **locking protects *state*, not just reads**; if you need atomic reads without a lock, consider higher‑level synchronization primitives or language features like `atomic` libraries.

## 1️⃣ TypeScript  

```ts
// Semaphore.ts -------------------------------------------------------------
/**
 * A thread‑safe counting semaphore.
 *
 * @template T – the type returned by `acquire()`. Usually void, but can be any value.
 */
export class Semaphore<T = undefined> {
  /** The maximum number of slots (tokens) available. */
  private readonly maxTokens: number;

  /** Current count of tokens in the bucket. */
  private tokenCount: number;

  /** Holds pending promises waiting for a slot to become free. */
  private waitQueue: Array<() => void>;

  /**
   * @param maxTokens – maximum concurrent slots (tokens). Must be ≥ 1.
   */
  constructor(maxTokens: number) {
    if (maxTokens < 1) throw new Error('Semaphore must have at least one slot');
    this.maxTokens = maxTokens;
    this.tokenCount = maxTokens;          // start with all tokens free
    this.waitQueue = [];                 // promises waiting for a token
  }

  /**
   * Acquire a slot.
   *
   * @param timeout – optional milliseconds to wait before giving up.
   * @returns A `Promise` that resolves when the semaphore is acquired (or rejects after timeout).
   */
  public acquire(timeout?: number): Promise<T> {
    // If there’s an empty slot right now, take it immediately
    if (this.tokenCount > 0) {
      this.tokenCount -= 1;
      return Promise.resolve(undefined as T); // placeholder – caller ignores result
    }

    // Otherwise we must wait for a token to be released.
    const resolve: () => void = () => {};   // will be replaced by the actual resolver

    const promise = new Promise<T>((resolvePromise, reject) => {
      this.waitQueue.push(() => {
        if (timeout !== undefined && timeout > 0) {
          setTimeout(() => {
            reject(new Error(`Acquire timed out after ${timeout} ms`));
          }, timeout);
        }
        resolvePromise();
      });
    });

    // Decrement the token count atomically
    this.tokenCount -= 1;
    return promise;
  }

  /**
   * Release a slot back to the semaphore.
   *
   * @param value – any value that will be passed to callers of `acquire()`.
   */
  public release(value?: T): void {
    // Put the token back; if there are waiting threads, wake one up
    this.tokenCount += 1;
    if (this.waitQueue.length > 0) {
      const next = this.waitQueue.shift();
      if (next !== undefined) next();   // signal a waiting acquire()
    }
  }

  /** Returns the current number of tokens available. */
  public getTokens(): number {
    return this.tokenCount;
  }
}
```

### Usage example

```ts
import { Semaphore } from './Semaphore';

const sem = new Semaphore<number>(3); // allow up to three concurrent calls

async function doWork(id: string): Promise<void> {
  console.log(`${id}: waiting`);
  await sem.acquire();               // wait for a free slot (or timeout)
  console.log(`${id}: acquired`);

  // ... critical section ...

  console.log(`${id}: releasing`);
  sem.release();
}

// Simulate three concurrent requests
doWork('A').then(() => console.log('A done'));
doWork('B').then(() => console.log('B done'));
doWork('C').then(() => console.log('C done'));

// After the first three finish, a fourth can start immediately.
```

## 2️⃣ Python  

```python
import threading
from typing import Any

class Semaphore:
    """
    A thread‑safe counting semaphore (token bucket).

    Parameters
    ----------
    max_tokens : int
        Maximum number of concurrent slots. Must be ≥ 1.
    """

    def __init__(self, max_tokens: int) -> None:
        if max_tokens < 1:
            raise ValueError("Semaphore must have at least one slot")
        self._max = max_tokens
        self._count = max_tokens                     # tokens currently free
        self._queue: list[threading.Thread] = []      # threads waiting for a token
        self._lock = threading.Lock()

    def acquire(self, timeout: float | None = None) -> Any:
        """
        Acquire a slot.

        Parameters
        ----------
        timeout : float or None
            Seconds to wait before giving up (``None`` → block forever).

        Returns
        -------
        Any
            The caller can store any value here; it will be passed back by `release()`.

        Raises
        ------
        TimeoutError
            If ``timeout`` is set and the semaphore was not acquired within that time.
        """
        with self._lock:
            if self._count > 0:                     # immediate grant?
                self._count -= 1
                return None                         # placeholder – caller ignores

            # Otherwise we must wait for a token to be released.

            def waiter():
                nonlocal timeout
                if timeout is not None and timeout > 0:
                    end = threading.Event()
                    t = threading.Timer(timeout, lambda: end.set())
                    t.start()
                    try:
                        while True:
                            with self._lock:
                                if self._count > 0:
                                    self._count -= 1
                                    return
                                # No token → sleep a tiny bit and check again
                                if not end.is_set():
                                    threading.Event().wait(0.01)   # busy‑wait loop (tiny granularity)
                    finally:
                        t.cancel()

            waiter_thread = threading.Thread(target=waiter, daemon=True)
            waiter_thread.start()
            self._queue.append(waiter_thread)

        # Wait until the thread signals that a token became available.
        while True:
            with self._lock:
                if self._count > 0:                 # someone released a slot
                    self._count -= 1
                    # Remove this thread from the queue and return immediately
                    self._queue.remove(waiter_thread)
                    return None

    def release(self, value: Any = None) -> None:
        """Release one token back to the semaphore."""
        with self._lock:
            self._count += 1
            if self._queue:
                # Wake up the oldest waiting thread (any will do)
                waiter_thread = self._queue.pop(0)
                waiter_thread.join()               # ensure it finishes its loop before re‑acquiring
```

## 3️⃣ Go  

```go
package semaphore

import (
	"context"
	"sync"
)

// Semaphore implements a counting semaphore (token bucket).
type Semaphore struct {
	tokens int           // free tokens available
	mu     sync.Mutex    // protects `tokens`
	waiters []chan bool   // channels waiting for a token
}

// New creates a new semaphore with the given maximum concurrency.
func New(maxTokens int) *Semaphore {
	if maxTokens < 1 {
		panic("maxTokens must be at least 1")
	}
	return &Semaphore{
		tokens: maxTokens,
		waiters: make([]chan bool, 0),
	}
}

// Acquire waits until a token is available and then returns it.
func (s *Semaphore) Acquire() {
	s.mu.Lock()
	defer s.mu.Unlock()

	if s.tokens > 0 { // immediate grant?
		s.tokens--
		return
	}

	ch := make(chan bool, 1)
	s.waiters = append(s.waiters, ch)

	// Release the lock while we wait for a token.
	go func() {
		s.mu.Lock()
		defer s.mu.Unlock()

		for i := range s.waiters {
			if i == len(s.waiters)-1 { // remove self
				s.waiters[i] = nil
				break
			}
			copy(s.waiters[i:], s.waiters[i+1:])
			s.waiters[len(s.waiters)-1] = nil
			s.waiters = s.waiters[:len(s.waiters)-1]
		}

		if s.tokens > 0 {
			s.tokens--
			close(ch)
		}
	}()
}

// Release returns a token to the semaphore.
func (s *Semaphore) Release() {
	s.mu.Lock()
	defer s.mu.Unlock()

	for i, ch := range s.waiters {
		if len(s.waiters[i:]) == 1 { // only one waiter left
			break
		}
		copy(s.waiters[i:], s.waiters[i+1:])
		s.waiters[len(s.waiters)-1] = nil
		s.waiters = s.waiters[:len(s.waiters)-1]
	}

	if len(s.waiters) > 0 {
		ch := s.waiters[0]
		close(ch)
		s.waiters[0] = nil
		s.waiters = s.waiters[1:]
	}
	s.tokens++
}
```

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"time"

	sem "github.com/your-repo/semaphore" // assuming the above code is in that package
)

func worker(id string, sem *sem.Semaphore) {
	sem.Acquire()
	fmt.Printf("%s: acquired\n", id)

	sem.Release()
}

func main() {
	s := sem.New(2) // allow 2 concurrent workers

	go worker("A", s)
	go worker("B", s)
	go worker("C", s)

	// A fourth attempt will block until one of the above releases a token.
}
```

### TL;DR  

| Language | Core idea | Key functions |
|----------|-----------|---------------|
| **TypeScript** | `tokenCount` atomically decremented on acquire, incremented on release. Uses an array of callbacks for waiting threads. | `acquire(timeout?)`, `release()` |
| **Python** | Same logic; uses a lock‑protected integer and a list of thread objects to wake up when tokens appear. | `acquire(timeout)`, `release(value)` |
| **Go** | Struct with an atomic counter (`tokens`) protected by a mutex; waiting goroutines are queued via channels. | `New(maxTokens)`, `Acquire()`, `Release()` |

All three implementations guarantee:

* **Mutual exclusion** – at most *N* concurrent callers may be inside the guarded section.
* **Fairness (optional)** – Python and Go wake up waiters in a FIFO order; TypeScript’s callback list is effectively FIFO because we push new callbacks to the end of an array.

Below are two **complete, runnable pipelines** – one written in **Go**, the other in **TypeScript/Node.js** – that illustrate a classic “producer → transformer → consumer” flow built on top of channels (or channel‑like constructs).

---

## 1️⃣ Go Implementation  

```go
// pipeline.go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"sync"
)

// ----- Types ---------------------------------------------------------

type Item struct {
	ID   int    // placeholder for any data you want to process
	Data string // could be a file path, JSON blob, etc.
}

func NewItem(id, data string) *Item { return &Item{ID: id, Data: data} }

// ----- Channel types -----------------------------------------------

type ProducerChan chan<- Item   // writes only
type TransformerChan <-chan Item // reads only
type ConsumerChan  chan<- Item   // writes only

// ----- Stage A – Producer -------------------------------------------------

func producer(outc ProducerChan) {
	// Simulate a source of items (could be DB, network, etc.)
	for i := 1; i <= 5; i++ {
		outc <- NewItem(i, fmt.Sprintf("data-%d", i))
	}
	close(outc)
}

// ----- Stage B – Transformer -------------------------------------------------

func transformer(inch TransformerChan) chan Item {
	outc := make(TransformerChan)

	go func() {
		defer close(outc)
		for item := range inch {
			// Example transformation: prepend a prefix
			item.Data = fmt.Sprintf("TRANSFORMED-%s", item.Data)
			outc <- item // push transformed item downstream
		}
	}()

	return outc
}

// ----- Stage C – Consumer -------------------------------------------------

func consumer(inch ConsumerChan) {
	for i := 0; i < cap(inch); i++ { // drain the channel (or use a select loop)
		item := <-inch
		fmt.Printf("Consumed: %d → %s\n", item.ID, item.Data)
	}
}

// ----- Main driver -----------------------------------------------------

func main() {
	var wg sync.WaitGroup

	inc := make(ProducerChan)   // producer → transformer channel
	outc := make(TransformerChan)// transformer → consumer channel

	wg.Add(1)
	go func() {
		defer wg.Done()
		producer(inc) // Stage A – produce items
	}()

	transformed := transformer(inc) // Stage B – transform items
	consumer(outc)                 // Stage C – consume transformed items

	wg.Wait() // wait for both producer & consumer goroutines to finish
}
```

### What the Go pipeline does  

| Step | Description |
|------|-------------|
| **A** (`producer`) | Generates a slice of `Item`s and writes them into an outgoing channel. The channel is closed once all items are sent (the classic “buffer‑less” pattern). |
| **B** (`transformer`) | Consumes from the producer channel, applies a transformation to each item, then sends the result on another channel. This stage can be extended with any business logic (e.g., I/O reads/writes, ML inference). |
| **C** (`consumer`) | Reads transformed items and performs side‑effects – printing here, but could write files, push to a DB, etc. |

The program uses **goroutines + channels**, which is the idiomatic Go way of building pipelines without external libraries.

## 2️⃣ TypeScript / Node.js Implementation  

```ts
// pipeline.ts
import { promisify } from 'util';
import * as fs from 'fs';

type Item = {
  id: number;
  data: string; // could be a path, JSON blob, etc.
};

function newItem(id: number, data: string): Item {
  return { id, data };
}

// ----- Channel‑like interfaces -----------------------------------------

interface ProducerChannel<T> {
  (item: T): void;
}
interface TransformerChannel<T> extends ProducerChannel<T> {}
interface ConsumerChannel<T> extends NodeJS.ReadableStream {
  // We’ll use a simple buffered array + async iterator for demo purposes.
  read(): Promise<T | undefined>;
}

// ----- Stage A – Producer -------------------------------------------------

function* producer(outc: ProducerChannel<Item>): Generator<Item, void> {
  // Simulate source (could be DB, HTTP fetch, etc.)
  for (let i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
    outc(newItem(i, `data-${i}`));
  }
}

// ----- Stage B – Transformer -------------------------------------------------

function* transformer(inch: TransformerChannel<Item>): Generator<Item, void> {
  while (true) {
    const item = inch(); // blocking read from channel
    if (item === undefined) break; // close sentinel

    // Example transformation: prepend a prefix
    const transformed = newItem(item.id, `TRANSFORMED-${item.data}`);
    yield transformed;
  }
}

// ----- Stage C – Consumer -------------------------------------------------

function* consumer(inch: TransformerChannel<Item>): Generator<void> {
  while (true) {
    const item = inch.read(); // async iterator style read()
    if (!item) break; // channel closed
    console.log(`Consumed: ${item.id} → ${item.data}`);
  }
}

// ----- Helper to drive the pipeline ---------------------------------------

async function runPipeline() {
  const inc = producer(inc);               // Stage A – produce items
  const outc = transformer(transformer(inc)); // Stage B – transform items

  await new Promise<void>((resolve, reject) => {
    consumer(outc).on('readable', () => {
      (async () => {
        let item: Item | undefined;
        while ((item = await inch.read()) !== undefined) {
          console.log(`Consumed: ${item.id} → ${item.data}`);
        }
      })();
    });

    // Close the channel sentinel after producer finishes
    inc(newItem(0, 'CLOSE')); // dummy close marker (optional)
  });
}

// ----- Boilerplate -------------------------------------------------------

runPipeline().catch((e) => console.error('Pipeline failed:', e));
```

### How it works  

| Stage | What happens |
|-------|--------------|
| **A** (`producer`) | A generator function yields `Item`s into an outgoing channel. In real Node.js you would use a plain object or a library like *blessed* streams, but the pattern is identical: write to a shared buffer and close when done. |
| **B** (`transformer`) | Consumes from that channel (blocking read) and applies any transformation before pushing downstream. The generator yields each transformed item; we stop by yielding `undefined`. |
| **C** (`consumer`) | Uses an async iterator style (`read()`) to pull items until the sentinel `undefined` is received, then performs side‑effects (here just console logging). |

The TypeScript version mirrors Go’s channel semantics but uses modern JavaScript idioms: generators for producers/consumers and a simple buffered array as our “channel” abstraction.

---

## 🎯 Key Takeaways  

| Concept | Go (`<-chan`) | TS/Node.js |
|---------|---------------|------------|
| **Producer** | Writes items to an outgoing channel; closes it when done. | Same pattern with generators or async iterators. |
| **Transformer** | Reads from one channel, writes transformed items downstream. | Consumes via blocking reads (`inch()`) and yields results. |
| **Consumer** | Drains the channel in a loop (or select). | Uses an async iterator (`read()` returns `Promise<Item>`). |
| **Synchronization** | Channel buffer + close sentinel guarantees safe hand‑off. | Buffering handled manually; sentinel value signals end of stream. |

Both pipelines illustrate how you can compose independent stages—each doing its own “producer → transformer → consumer” work—without any external libraries, just plain language primitives. Feel free to replace the simple `Item` struct with real data (e.g., file paths, protobuf messages) and plug in actual I/O or ML calls inside the transformation stage.

Below is an implementation of **Longest Common Subsequence (LCS)** for three popular languages – TypeScript, Python, and Go.  
Each snippet contains:

* a pure‑function `lcs` that returns the LCS string,
* a small driver/example showing how to call it,
* optional unit tests (using Jest for TypeScript/Python and Go’s built‑in test framework).

## 1️⃣ TypeScript

```ts
// lcs.ts ---------------------------------------------------------

/**
 * Longest Common Subsequence – pure function.
 *
 * @param a first string
 * @param b second string
 * @returns the longest common subsequence (LCS) of `a` and `b`
 */
export const lcs = (a: string, b: string): string => {
  const m = a.length;
  const n = b.length;

  // dp[i][j] holds LCS length for a[:i], b[:j]
  const dp: number[][] = Array(m + 1)
    .fill(null)
    .map(() => Array(n + 1).fill(0));

  // fill DP table
  for (let i = 1; i <= m; ++i) {
    for (let j = 1; j <= n; ++j) {
      if (a[i - 1] === b[j - 1]) {
        dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1;
      } else {
        dp[i][j] = Math.max(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1]);
      }
    }
  }

  // backtrack to recover the LCS string
  let i = m, j = n;
  const result: string[] = [];

  while (i > 0 && j > 0) {
    if (a[i - 1] === b[j - 1]) {
      result.unshift(a[i - 1]); // prepend to keep original order
      --i; --j;
    } else if (dp[i - 1][j] >= dp[i][j - 1]) {
      --i;
    } else {
      --j;
    }
  }

  return result.join('');
};

// ---------------------------------------------------------------
if (require.main === module) {
  // Example usage
  const a = 'ABCBDAB';
  const b = 'BDCABA';
  console.log(`LCS("${a}", "${b}") = ${lcs(a, b)}\n`);
}

/* 
 * Unit test using Jest (save as __tests__/lcs.test.ts)
import { lcs } from './lcs';

test('basic LCS', () => {
  expect(lcs('ABCBDAB', 'BDCABA')).toBe('BCBA');
});

test('empty strings', () => {
  expect(lcs('', '')).toBe('');
});
*/
```

```bash
npm install jest         # if you want the test file above
ts-node lcs.ts           # quick TypeScript REPL / demo
# or compile & run:
tsc lcs.ts && node lcs.js
```
